sentences.text: Right now, as you watch this, the Moon is falling towards the Earth.
So why doesn't it ever hit us?
And what does it have to do with an apple?
By the end of this film, you'll know how a young man in a farmhouse garden, an imaginary cannon and one careful sum showed that the pull that drops an apple also holds the Moon in the sky.
For thousands of years, people believed the sky followed different rules from the Earth.
Down here, things fell.
A stone dropped, a cup tipped, a rider fell from a horse.
But up there, the Moon, the Sun and the planets moved in perfect circles, for ever, and never fell at all.
Why should a stone fall, but not the Moon?
It was one of the oldest mysteries in the world.
Picture yourself on a clear night in sixteen sixty-five.
You would see the Moon rise over the fields, huge and silent.
You would feel the cold ground under your feet.
And if you dropped a stone, you would hear it thud.
Would you ever think that the stone and the Moon were doing the same thing?
One young man did.
And it started in a year when the whole country was afraid.

parts.chapter_card: An Apple in a Plague Year

sentences.text: In sixteen sixty-five, a terrible plague swept through England.
To keep students safe, the university at Cambridge closed its doors.
And a young student called Isaac Newton went home, to his family's farmhouse in the village of Woolsthorpe.
He had been born in that same house, on Christmas Day, sixteen forty-two.
His father had died a few months before.
Newton was so tiny, his mother later said, that he could have fitted inside a quart pot.
For almost two years, he worked alone.
He studied light, invented new kinds of mathematics, and asked questions no one had asked before.
Many years later, when he was an old man, Newton told a friend how one of those questions began.
He was sitting in the garden, thinking, when an apple fell from a tree.
The apple didn't hit him on the head.
That part was added later.
But it made him wonder.
The apple always falls straight down, towards the centre of the Earth.
The pull that drags it down works at the top of the tree.
It works at the top of a tall tower, and at the top of a mountain.
So how far up does it reach?
Could it reach all the way to the Moon?
It was an extraordinary idea.
If the Earth was pulling on the Moon, then the Moon should be falling.
But it was still up there, night after night.
So what was holding it up?
Newton's answer was so simple it is easy to miss.
The Moon isn't held up at all.
It really is falling.
It just never lands.
To explain it, he imagined a cannon, on top of a mountain so tall it poked above the air.
Fire a cannonball sideways, gently, and it curves down and hits the ground near the bottom of the mountain.
Fire it faster, and it flies further before it lands.
Now imagine firing it so fast that, as it falls, the round Earth curves away beneath it, just as quickly.
What would you see?
The ball keeps falling, and keeps missing the ground.
It falls all the way around the world, and comes back to the mountain.
That is an orbit.
Not something floating, but something falling, and moving sideways so fast that it never hits.
And that's what the Moon is doing.
Every second, it moves sideways about a kilometre, and falls a tiny bit towards the Earth.
Sideways and down, sideways and down, for ever.
But an idea isn't proof.
If the same pull holds the Moon and drops the apple, Newton should be able to calculate one from the other.
Could he?
Newton worked out that a pull like this should get weaker with distance.
Twice as far away, it should be four times weaker.
Three times as far, nine times weaker.
Why would it work like that?
Think of a can of spray paint.
Hold it close to a wall and you get a small, dark spot.
Step back twice as far, and the same paint spreads over a patch four times as big, so every part of it gets only a quarter as much.
Newton's pull spreads out in the same way.
The Moon is about sixty times further from the centre of the Earth than you are.
So the pull on the Moon should be sixty times sixty weaker.
Three thousand six hundred times weaker.
Then came the beautiful part.
In one second, an apple falls about five metres.
If the pull on the Moon is 3,600 times weaker, then in one minute, the Moon should fall about the same distance, five metres, along its curve.
Newton checked it against the real Moon.
Years later, he wrote that the two answered pretty nearly.
The apple and the Moon were obeying the same rule.
But Newton was a careful, private man, and his numbers weren't yet perfect.
He put the idea aside for almost twenty years.
Then, in sixteen eighty-four, a young astronomer called Edmond Halley came to see him in Cambridge.
Halley asked him a question.
If the Sun pulled on the planets with a force that got weaker in just this way, what path would they follow?
An ellipse, Newton said at once.
He had worked it out years before.
Halley was amazed, and he begged Newton to write it all down.
The result, three years later, was one of the most important books ever written.
Newton called it the Principia.
And because the Royal Society had spent its money on a book about fish, Halley paid to print it himself.
Newton's law didn't stop at the Moon.
The same pull keeps the Earth falling around the Sun, and the planets, and the moons of Jupiter.
The Moon even pulls back on the Earth, and lifts the oceans into tides.
Halley used Newton's law to work out the path of a bright comet, and he made a bold prediction.
It would come back in seventeen fifty-eight.
Halley died years before it was due.
But on Christmas night, seventeen fifty-eight, the comet appeared in the sky, right on time.
It has carried his name ever since.
And you can see Newton's cannon at work today.
The International Space Station flies around the Earth at about twenty-eight thousand kilometres an hour.
It's not floating above gravity.
It's falling, all the time, just like the Moon.
The astronauts inside float because they're falling too, right along with it.
Imagine being up there, with an apple drifting in front of your face.
It looks as if gravity has switched off.
But it hasn't.
You, the apple and the station are all falling together, around the world.
Why was this so groundbreaking?
Because for the first time, the heavens and the Earth followed the same rules.
The force that drops a cup off your table is the same force that steers the planets.
One law, written in mathematics, that works everywhere we have ever looked.
So tonight, if you can see the Moon, take a moment to look at it.
It is falling towards you, right now.
And it will keep on missing.
An apple, a cannon and a sum.
Together, they pulled the heavens down to Earth.
But gravity can bring more than apples down.
Sixty-six million years ago, something far bigger fell out of the sky.
And the clue was hidden in a thin layer of clay.
